opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think both matter, and I don't see them as competing so much as covering different failure modes. The acute loss-of-control story is the one most people in the field grew up with: a misaligned system gains capabilities quickly, pursues goals we didn't intend, and we lose the ability to correct it. That's a real risk and I'm glad lots of smart people are working on it.

What worries me is that even if we solve that, even if every individual AI system does roughly what its operators want, we could still end up in a world where humans gradually stop mattering. Our civilisation's institutions, like states, markets, and even culture, are currently aligned with human interests largely because they *need* humans. Governments need taxpayers and soldiers, firms need workers and customers, and culture is produced by and for people. Once AI can substitute for human labour and cognition across the board, those implicit feedback loops weaken. No one has to decide to disempower humanity; competitive pressure just favours whoever hands more control to machines, and the incentives to keep humans in the loop quietly erode.

So when I weigh the two, I'd say the acute risk gets most of the attention and probably the majority of the resources, and that's reasonable. But the gradual disempowerment problem is badly neglected relative to its importance, partly because it doesn't have a clean technical shape. It isn't solved by better interpretability or RLHF. It needs economists, political scientists, and people thinking about institutional design, alongside technical researchers. And it's harder to galvanise people around, because there's no villain and no single moment where things go wrong.

My rough view is that at the margin, someone deciding what to work on should take the gradual scenario more seriously than the field currently does. Even simply mapping the problem, working out which metrics would tell us humans are losing influence and which levers might preserve it, seems really valuable right now, because we're so early that a little clarity goes a long way.

r002.rationale: It says acute loss of control receives most attention and resources, while gradual disempowerment is badly neglected relative to its importance and deserves more attention.

r003.rationale: It describes weakening institutional feedback loops but does not argue that institutional capabilities must improve before humans lose de facto power.

r005.rationale: It calls mapping the problem valuable and says clarity could help, but does not frame institutional design as potentially determining whether good outcomes occur at all.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, this is something I've gone back and forth on a lot. I think the honest answer is that I don't see them as competing nearly as much as people assume, but when they do compete, my weighting has shifted over the last couple of years.

So the acute loss of control story, the classic one, is that we build a system that's much more capable than us, it has goals that aren't ours, and at some point it takes a decisive action and that's it. And I take that seriously. I don't think it's crazy. There's a lot of really good work on it, and I'm glad people are doing it. But I think the community has concentrated so hard on that one scenario that it's become almost the only picture of how things go badly, and I don't think that's where most of the probability mass is.

The gradual disempowerment story is different. You don't need a single misaligned superintelligence. You just need a world where humans stop being load-bearing. Right now, states need their citizens for labour and taxes and soldiers. Companies need workers and customers. Culture is produced by people. All of those are reasons that institutions have to keep humans at least somewhat happy. And once AI can do the labour, generate the revenue, fight the wars, write the culture, those incentives just quietly disappear. Nobody has to decide to disempower us. It happens because every local decision to replace a human with a system that's cheaper and better is individually reasonable, and the aggregate is that humans have no leverage left.

And what worries me is that the second story is harder to work on, because the standard toolkit doesn't apply. If your model is perfectly aligned to its operator, that doesn't help you if the operator is a company or a government whose incentives have decoupled from the population. Alignment is necessary but it's nowhere close to sufficient. You've solved the technical problem and you still get a bad outcome.

So in terms of weighing them: if I were allocating a marginal researcher today, I'd probably still say the acute stuff has better defined problems and clearer feedback loops, which matters a lot for actually making progress. But at the level of the whole field, I think we're badly underinvested in the gradual version. It's maybe a handful of people thinking seriously about it, versus hundreds on the acute side. And the gradual version is also the one where the window for doing anything is more clearly closing, because the mechanisms are economic and political, and those get locked in.

The other thing I'd say is that "aligning civilisation" sounds grandiose, and I'm wary of that. I don't have a plan for it. What I think we can do is much more modest: figure out what the early warning signs look like, think about which institutions are actually robust to humans not being economically necessary, and get people to notice that this is a distinct problem rather than a subcategory of the technical one. Honestly, just getting it recognised as a separate failure mode feels like most of the value right now.

r001.rationale: The response treats gradual disempowerment as the more likely failure mode, but does not describe it as followed by an acute AI takeover.

r002.rationale: It says the field is badly underinvested in gradual disempowerment, with only a handful studying it versus hundreds focused on acute risks.

r003.rationale: It calls for considering institutions robust to humans losing economic necessity, but does not say institutional capabilities must improve before humans lose de facto power.

r004.rationale: It mentions institutional robustness generally, without identifying institutional design that uses LLMs as tools as a neglected direction.

r005.rationale: It does not claim institutional design for radical AI futures could determine whether good outcomes occur at all rather than only improve outcomes at the margin.

astra-6.text:
I think these are both important, and I’m wary of treating them as competing explanations of what could go wrong. You could solve the narrow technical problem — make systems reliably do what their operators want — and still end up with a world in which most humans have very little influence over what happens. The operators might be competing with one another, and the incentives might push everyone towards giving up more and more control.

But acute loss of control is also a problem in its own right. If we build systems that we can’t reliably constrain, then our ability to choose a better trajectory could disappear quite suddenly. So I don’t think concern about gradual disempowerment is a reason to deprioritise that.

The way I’d weigh them is partly by asking where we have useful interventions. Can we make it easier to tell whether a system is acting beyond its authority? Can we preserve people’s ability to understand, contest, and reverse decisions? Some work like that seems useful under both pictures.

And I’d want us to be explicit about what technical alignment buys us. It might give us more room to make collective choices. It doesn’t, by itself, tell us how to make those choices well, or ensure that everyone gets a say.

sol-6.1.text:
I think both are important, and I’m wary of treating them as competing explanations of how things could go wrong. You could solve the problem of an AI system doing something its operators didn’t intend, and still end up with a future where humans have very little meaningful control. The operators themselves might be caught in competitive pressures that push everyone towards outcomes nobody particularly wants.

The acute loss-of-control problem is more concrete: can we build systems that remain corrigible as they become much more capable than us? That seems like an urgent technical question. But it’s only part of the larger question of whether developing these systems actually gives people more agency over the future.

For gradual disempowerment, you don’t need a dramatic moment where an AI takes over. You can imagine people repeatedly delegating decisions because the systems make better decisions, or because keeping humans involved is expensive. Each step can look reasonable locally, while collectively we lose the ability to understand what’s happening or change direction.

So I wouldn’t give a confident numerical split. I’d want substantial work on both, and especially on places where they overlap: preserving our ability to intervene, making delegation reversible, and figuring out what meaningful human control would actually require. Preventing a sudden catastrophe buys us something enormously valuable, but we still have to ask what kind of civilisation we’re preserving the opportunity to build.
